test: Build job-level economics for order jobs: revenue = invoiced amount (ex freight) per job, material = sum of material PO amounts on the job, labour = clocked hours on the job. Compute value-add (revenue - material) per clocked hour, aggregated by customer, part family, order-quantity band and year (and family x qty band). Compare with the shop average and with a fully loaded rate = GL (direct + indirect labour + overhead + benefits) / clocked hours per year. Look for groups with meaningful revenue (e.g. >=1% of revenue or >=$100k) below the loaded rate, and check whether they persist across years.
support: A group (part family, small-quantity band, or customers) carrying a meaningful share of revenue has value-add per clocked hour below the fully loaded rate, persistently across several years, not just in one steel-spike year.
weaken: Value-add per hour stays within a tight band around the shop average for every customer, family and quantity band with meaningful revenue, and all are above the loaded rate; any low groups are tiny or single-year.
expect: Mostly weaken (about 65%). Segment and customer views were tight. The most likely place for a real tail is small-quantity orders, where setup hours dominate, unless pricing already reflects setup. Steel-spike years (2021-2022) may compress margins, but the invoice uplift may offset that.
